Emission Factors, Second Edition, U.S. EPA, AP-42, Research Triangle Park, NC, December 1975, section D.1.6., Credit for Inspection and Maintenance Program, page D.1-17: "A 10 percent reduction in CO and HC can be applied to all model year vehicles starting the year I/M is introduced." The EOEA comment references techniques published in May 1977 and after the publication of our technical report.
Apparently, utilization of the recently-released revised mobile source emission factors by the EPA and the revised clean air act amendment would increase the emissions reported in our final report. It is our understanding, however, that the regulations are still in draft form. Consequently calculations have not been made because of the status of the regulations and additional oost which was not budgeted to accomplish this.
It should be noted that the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) letter stating that the DEIS adequately addressed the project's potential impacts in regard to air, water, and noise was dated August 9, 1977.
Traffic Impacts:
The CRA's consultant disagrees with the statement that the 17 percent and 29 percent increases in traffic on Broadway and Third Street mean that the congestion and air pollution on those streets would be increased equivalently. The use of these percentages for such precise areas as particular intersections is inappropriate. However, the CRA agrees that traffic congestion in the area is likely. HUD also notes that the existing conditions are already congested. As identified in the report, operational measures which would minimize the impact of the increased traffic by accommodating both the increased traffic and the estimated existing traffic. As listed on page 74, of Chapter 5 of Part II, these measures include traffic signal timing adjustments, traffic response signal controls, clearance of curb lanes on intersection approaches, enforced parking prohibitions or peak hour restrictions, peak hour truck loading restrictions, one way streets and improved access.
With regard to expanding the traffic study to include peak hour traffic flows beyond the project impact area, HUD feels that this is unecessary, since they have been identified, in the report, the critical information for understanding the project.
Pedestrian and Bicycle Access:
Preparation of the circulation plan for pedestrian movement as well as bicycle access appears to HUD to be a design step at a level of detail beyond the present planning for Kendall Square development.
Aesthetics:
HUD notes the agreement on the part of the EOEA with the aesthetics analysis presented in the report.
